short: A tax the government charges on what a person or business earns in a year, such as salary, business profit, interest or gains.
kid: When you earn coins for helping at the lemonade stand, you give a few of them to the town. The town uses them to fix roads and run schools for everyone.
detail: Income tax is a direct tax on the income earned by individuals, Hindu undivided families, firms and companies over a year. In India it is levied by the Centre, under the Income-tax Act 1961 for income earned up to March 2026 and the Income-tax Act 2025 from April 2026. Income is grouped under five heads: salary, house property, business or profession, capital gains and other sources. Total income, after allowed deductions, is taxed at slab rates for individuals and at flat rates for companies (usually called corporate tax), with surcharge and cess on top. Personal income tax is now one of the Centre's largest revenue sources, so Budget changes to slabs or deductions affect household spending and consumption stocks. A common confusion: tax is charged on taxable income after deductions, not on gross salary.
example: Say Asha earns a salary of ₹10 lakh and ₹40,000 of bank interest in FY 2025-26. Under the new regime her taxable income is ₹10 lakh + ₹40,000 - ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹9.65 lakh. Because this is below ₹12 lakh, the Section 87A rebate wipes out her tax under the rules as of 2025.
formula: Taxable income = Gross total income - Allowed deductions

short: A tax that the person or company it is charged on must pay and bear themselves, such as income tax or corporate tax.
kid: If you earn ten sweets and must hand one to your teacher yourself, that is a direct tax. Nobody else can hand it over for you.
detail: A direct tax is levied on, paid by and borne by the same person: the taxpayer cannot shift the burden to someone else through prices. Examples are personal income tax, corporate tax and capital gains tax; in India, securities transaction tax is also classed as a direct tax and administered by the Central Board of Direct Taxes. Direct taxes are usually linked to ability to pay, which makes them suited to progressive rates. In recent years direct taxes have made up more than half of the Centre's gross tax revenue, and direct tax collection data, especially advance tax, is read as a signal of corporate profits and household incomes. The common confusion: a tax is not direct just because it is paid straight to the government. GST is deposited by businesses but borne by consumers, so it is indirect.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns a profit of ₹100 crore and pays corporate tax at, say, 25%, which is ₹25 crore. That money comes out of ABC's own profit; it cannot be added to a customer's bill the way a shop adds GST, so it is a direct tax.

short: A tax collected by a seller or importer and passed on to the buyer in the price, such as GST or customs duty.
kid: When you buy a lollipop, the shop adds a tiny extra bit to the price. The shop keeps that bit safe and later gives it to the town.
detail: An indirect tax is collected by one party, usually a business, but its burden falls on another, usually the final consumer, because it is built into prices. Goods and Services Tax (GST), customs duty on imports and excise duty on fuel and tobacco are the main Indian examples. Indirect taxes are easier to collect and harder to evade, but they are often regressive: a poorer household spends a larger share of its income on taxed goods, so it pays a larger share of its income in tax. In India, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) runs central GST, customs and excise. For markets, GST or customs rate changes can shift the prices, demand and margins of whole sectors, as the September 2025 GST cuts did for cars and consumer goods. The confusion to avoid: the business files and pays the tax, but the customer bears it.
example: Say a shop sells headphones for ₹2,000 plus 18% GST, so the buyer pays ₹2,360. The shop passes the ₹360 on to the government (after claiming credit for GST on its own purchases), but it was the buyer who bore the whole ₹360 through the price.
formula: Price paid by buyer = Pre-tax price x (1 + Tax rate)

short: A tax that takes a bigger share of income from those who earn more. Regressive taxes do the reverse; flat taxes charge one rate.
kid: A child with ten sweets puts two in the sharing jar, and a child with two sweets puts in none. Those who have more share a bigger part.
detail: A progressive tax has an average rate that rises with income, usually through slabs where higher slices of income face higher marginal rates. India's personal income tax is progressive: under the rules as of 2025 the new regime runs from nil up to 30%. A regressive tax takes a larger share of a poorer person's income, which is how consumption taxes like GST often work in practice, since poorer households spend more of what they earn. A flat (proportional) tax charges one rate at every income level; Estonia and several other Eastern European countries have used flat income taxes. Economists debate the trade-off between fairness and the incentive to earn and invest. The common confusion: crossing into a higher slab does not raise the tax on all your income, only on the part above the slab's starting point.
example: Under the new-regime slabs for FY 2025-26, taxable income of ₹20 lakh attracts ₹2 lakh of tax before cess: an average rate of 10%, even though the top slice is taxed at 20%. At ₹40 lakh the tax is ₹7.8 lakh, an average rate of 19.5%. Because the average rate rises with income, the tax is progressive.
formula: Average tax rate = Total tax / Taxable income

short: A band of income taxed at one rate; income is cut into slabs, and each slice is taxed at its own slab's rate.
kid: Picture stacking blocks. The bottom blocks are free, the next few cost one sticker each, and the top blocks cost two stickers each.
detail: An income-tax slab, called a tax bracket in most countries, is a range of income charged at a fixed marginal rate. Taxable income is split into slices, each slice is taxed at its slab's rate, and the results are added. Under the rules as of 2025, the new-regime slabs for FY 2025-26 are: up to ₹4 lakh nil, ₹4-8 lakh 5%, ₹8-12 lakh 10%, ₹12-16 lakh 15%, ₹16-20 lakh 20%, ₹20-24 lakh 25% and above ₹24 lakh 30%. The old regime keeps fewer, steeper slabs (nil, 5%, 20% and 30%) with higher exemption limits for senior citizens. Slab changes come in the Union Budget. The big confusion: moving into a higher slab taxes only the income above that slab's starting point at the higher rate, never all your income, so a pay rise never cuts take-home pay just by crossing a slab.
example: Taxable income of ₹14.25 lakh under the new regime for FY 2025-26 is taxed as: first ₹4 lakh nil, next ₹4 lakh at 5% = ₹20,000, next ₹4 lakh at 10% = ₹40,000, and the last ₹2.25 lakh at 15% = ₹33,750. The total is ₹93,750, plus 4% cess of ₹3,750, so ₹97,500.
formula: Tax before cess = Sum over slabs of (Income falling in the slab x Slab rate)

short: India's default personal income tax system since FY 2023-24, with lower slab rates but almost none of the old deductions and exemptions.
kid: You can play a simple game with fewer rules and smaller costs, or an old game with lots of special bonus cards. Everyone gets the simple game unless they ask for the old one.
detail: The new tax regime, in Section 115BAC of the Income-tax Act 1961 (Section 202 of the 2025 Act), arrived in Budget 2020 as an option and became the default from FY 2023-24. It offers lower, wider slabs but removes most exemptions and deductions, such as Section 80C, 80D, HRA and interest on a self-occupied home loan. Under the rules as of 2025 it still allows a ₹75,000 standard deduction for salaried people, the employer's NPS contribution, and a Section 87A rebate that makes taxable income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free. Salaried taxpayers can choose either regime each year when filing; those with business income can switch only in limited cases. It weakens the pull of tax-saving products such as ELSS and insurance. The confusion to avoid: the new regime is not always cheaper; someone with large deductions may still pay less under the old one.
example: Say a salaried person earns ₹12 lakh in FY 2025-26. Under the new regime taxable income is ₹12 lakh - ₹75,000 = ₹11.25 lakh, and slab tax is ₹20,000 + ₹32,500 = ₹52,500. The Section 87A rebate (up to ₹60,000) cancels all of it, so the tax is nil.

short: India's older personal income tax system, with higher slab rates but many deductions and exemptions, such as 80C, 80D and HRA.
kid: This is the old game with lots of special bonus cards. If you collect enough cards by saving and planning, you get to share fewer sweets.
detail: The old tax regime is the original structure of personal income tax that applied to everyone before the new regime arrived. Under the rules as of 2025 its slabs for individuals under 60 are nil up to ₹2.5 lakh, 5% up to ₹5 lakh, 20% up to ₹10 lakh and 30% above, with higher exemption limits for senior citizens. In exchange for steeper rates it allows many deductions and exemptions: Section 80C investments up to ₹1.5 lakh, 80D health insurance, HRA, leave travel allowance, home loan interest and a ₹50,000 standard deduction. Since FY 2023-24 a taxpayer must actively opt for it; otherwise the new regime applies. It suits people with large deductions, such as a big home loan plus rent and insurance. The common mistake is assuming tax-saving investments always save tax: they help only if you actually choose the old regime.
example: Say a person earns a ₹12 lakh salary and claims ₹1.5 lakh under 80C, ₹25,000 under 80D and the ₹50,000 standard deduction in FY 2025-26. Taxable income is ₹9.75 lakh, slab tax is ₹12,500 + ₹95,000 = ₹1,07,500, and with 4% cess the bill is ₹1,11,800. Under the new regime the same salary would pay nil, so this person is better off switching.

short: A flat amount that salaried people and pensioners can subtract from their salary income before tax, without showing any bills or proof.
kid: Before counting how many sweets you must share, everyone gets to keep a small handful first, no questions asked.
detail: The standard deduction is a fixed deduction from income under the head 'Salaries', including pension, that needs no proof of spending. India reintroduced it in Budget 2018 in place of the separate transport allowance and medical reimbursement exemptions. Under the rules as of 2025 it is ₹75,000 in the new regime and ₹50,000 in the old regime, and family pensioners get a separate deduction (up to ₹25,000 in the new regime). Employers apply it automatically in Form 16 and it flows into the return. Raising it is a quick way for a government to cut tax for salaried people without touching slabs, so it often features in Budget speeches. The US also has a standard deduction, but there it is an alternative to itemising deductions and applies to all filers. The confusion to avoid: in India it reduces only salary or pension income, not business, rental or capital gains income.
example: Say a person's gross salary for FY 2025-26 is ₹10 lakh. Under the new regime, taxable salary becomes ₹10 lakh - ₹75,000 = ₹9.25 lakh. Under the old regime it would be ₹10 lakh - ₹50,000 = ₹9.5 lakh, before 80C and other deductions.
formula: Taxable salary = Gross salary - Standard deduction - Other allowed deductions

short: An Indian tax deduction for approved savings such as provident funds, tax-saving mutual funds and life insurance, open only under the old regime.
kid: If you put some of your coins in your piggy bank, the grown-ups let you share fewer sweets. Saving gets a little reward.
detail: Section 80C of the Income-tax Act 1961 (Section 123 of the 2025 Act) lets individuals and HUFs reduce taxable income by amounts paid into specified savings and expenses, capped at ₹1.5 lakh a year under the rules as of 2025, a limit unchanged since 2014. Eligible items include employee EPF contributions, the Public Provident Fund, ELSS mutual funds, life insurance premiums, home loan principal repayment, children's tuition fees, five-year tax-saving bank deposits, National Savings Certificates and Sukanya Samriddhi deposits. It is available only under the old regime. Because many people rush to invest before 31 March, 80C drives seasonal flows into ELSS funds and insurance. The common confusion: 80C reduces taxable income, not the tax itself, so the saving depends on your slab; at 20%, a full ₹1.5 lakh deduction saves ₹30,000 plus cess.
example: Say an old-regime taxpayer in the 20% slab puts ₹1 lakh in PPF, ₹50,000 in an ELSS fund and pays a ₹30,000 life insurance premium. That is ₹1.8 lakh, but the deduction is capped at ₹1.5 lakh. Tax falls by 20% of ₹1.5 lakh = ₹30,000, or ₹31,200 including 4% cess.
formula: Tax saved = Eligible 80C amount (up to the cap) x Marginal tax rate x (1 + Cess rate)

short: An Indian tax deduction for health insurance premiums and preventive health check-ups for yourself, your family and your parents, open only under the old regime.
kid: If you pay a little each year so a doctor will help when you are sick, the grown-ups let you share fewer sweets. Staying safe gets a small reward.
detail: Section 80D of the Income-tax Act 1961, carried into the 2025 Act under a new section number, lets individuals and HUFs deduct medical insurance premiums. Under the rules as of 2025 the limit is ₹25,000 a year for self, spouse and dependent children (₹50,000 if any of them is a senior citizen), plus a separate ₹25,000 for parents (₹50,000 if a parent is a senior citizen), so the maximum is ₹1 lakh. Up to ₹5,000 of preventive health check-up costs fits within these limits, and senior citizens without insurance can claim medical bills instead. Premiums must be paid by a non-cash method. It applies only in the old regime. It is a policy nudge towards health cover in a country with low insurance penetration. The confusion to avoid: 80D is separate from, and in addition to, the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit.
example: Say an old-regime taxpayer under 60 pays ₹22,000 for a family floater policy and ₹40,000 for a policy covering both parents, who are senior citizens. The deduction is ₹22,000 (within the ₹25,000 limit) + ₹40,000 (within the ₹50,000 limit) = ₹62,000. In the 30% slab that saves ₹18,600 before cess.

short: A reduction in the final tax bill for resident individuals with modest taxable income, which can bring their income tax down to zero.
kid: If you have only a few sweets, the grown-ups say you don't need to share any. They hand back whatever you were going to share.
detail: A rebate is subtracted from the tax computed on income, unlike a deduction, which is subtracted from income. Section 87A gives resident individuals a rebate equal to their tax, up to a cap, when taxable income is within a threshold. Under the rules as of 2025 (FY 2025-26), the new regime allows a rebate of up to ₹60,000 when taxable income is up to ₹12 lakh, so no tax is due; with the ₹75,000 standard deduction, a salary up to ₹12.75 lakh pays nothing. The old regime allows up to ₹12,500 for income up to ₹5 lakh. Just above the threshold, marginal relief ensures the extra tax never exceeds the extra income. The rebate does not cover tax on special-rate income such as equity capital gains. The common confusion: the rebate makes tax nil, but the income is not exempt, so you may still need to file a return.
example: Say a resident under the new regime has taxable income of ₹12.1 lakh with no salary in FY 2025-26. Slab tax would be ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + ₹1,500 = ₹61,500 and no rebate applies above ₹12 lakh, but marginal relief caps the tax at ₹10,000, the amount by which income exceeds ₹12 lakh. At exactly ₹12 lakh, the ₹60,000 of tax would be fully rebated to nil.
formula: Tax after rebate = Tax on total income - Rebate, where Rebate = Lower of (Tax on total income, Cap) if income is within the threshold

short: A part of salary paid by employers to cover rent; part of it can be tax-free under India's old regime if you actually pay rent.
kid: A grown-up's boss gives some extra coins to help pay for the house they live in. If those coins really go to the house owner, some of them don't count when sharing.
detail: House rent allowance (HRA) is a salary component meant to help employees pay rent. Under Section 10(13A) of the 1961 Act and the related rule, the exempt part is the lowest of three amounts: the actual HRA received; rent paid minus 10% of salary; and 50% of salary for those living in Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata or Chennai, or 40% elsewhere, where salary means basic pay plus dearness allowance (under the rules as of 2025). Only the exempt part escapes tax; the rest is taxed as salary. The exemption is available only under the old regime and needs rent receipts, plus the landlord's PAN if yearly rent exceeds ₹1 lakh. Someone who pays rent but gets no HRA may claim a smaller deduction under Section 80GG. Common errors: assuming the whole HRA is tax-free, or claiming it while living in one's own house.
example: Say an employee in Delhi has basic salary of ₹6 lakh a year, receives HRA of ₹2.4 lakh and pays rent of ₹2.16 lakh (₹18,000 a month). The three limits are ₹2.4 lakh, ₹2.16 lakh - ₹60,000 = ₹1.56 lakh, and 50% of ₹6 lakh = ₹3 lakh. The exempt HRA is the lowest, ₹1.56 lakh, and the remaining ₹84,000 is taxable under the old regime.
formula: HRA exemption = Lowest of (Actual HRA received, Rent paid - 10% of salary, 50% of salary in the four metros or 40% elsewhere)

short: An extra tax charged as a percentage of the income tax itself, applied only to people and companies with high incomes.
kid: Children with a really big pile of sweets share a little extra on top of their usual share.
detail: A surcharge is a tax on tax: it is calculated on the income tax payable, not on income. Under the rules as of 2025, individuals pay 10% of their tax when income exceeds ₹50 lakh, 15% above ₹1 crore, 25% above ₹2 crore and 37% above ₹5 crore in the old regime, while the new regime caps it at 25%. Surcharge on dividends and on capital gains from listed equity is capped at 15%. Companies pay 7% or 12% depending on income, or a flat 10% under the concessional 22% corporate rate. Marginal relief stops someone just above a threshold from paying more extra tax than their extra income. Unlike ordinary income tax, surcharge revenue is not shared with the states. The confusion to avoid: a 10% surcharge raises your tax by 10%, not your tax rate by 10 percentage points.
example: Say an individual under the new regime has taxable income of ₹60 lakh in FY 2025-26. Slab tax is ₹13.8 lakh; the 10% surcharge adds ₹1.38 lakh, making ₹15.18 lakh. The 4% cess on that adds ₹60,720, for a total of ₹15,78,720.
formula: Surcharge = Income tax x Surcharge rate

short: An extra tax raised for a stated purpose, such as health or education, usually charged as a small percentage on top of another tax.
kid: After you share your sweets, you drop one more into a special jar that only buys books and medicine for the class.
detail: A cess is a levy the Union government imposes for a declared purpose, often as a percentage of an existing tax. On income tax, a 4% health and education cess is charged on tax plus surcharge under the rules as of 2025, so every taxpayer who owes tax pays it. Other examples include cesses on crude oil, fuel and imports, such as the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess. Under GST, a compensation cess on luxury and sin goods funded payments to states for revenue losses after 2017; it was largely removed in the September 2025 GST overhaul. Cess and surcharge revenue is not shared with states through the Finance Commission formula, which is why states object when the Centre leans on them. The common confusion: a 4% cess means 4% of the tax, not 4% of income.
example: Say an individual's income tax plus surcharge comes to ₹2,50,000. The 4% health and education cess adds ₹10,000, taking the total payable to ₹2,60,000.
formula: Health and education cess = 4% x (Income tax + Surcharge), at the rate as of 2025

short: Tax that a payer cuts from a payment, like salary, interest or rent, and deposits with the government on the receiver's behalf.
kid: Before your friend hands you ten sweets for helping, they put one aside for the class jar. You get nine, and the jar knows that one came from you.
detail: Tax deducted at source (TDS) makes the payer, such as an employer, bank, tenant or company, deduct tax when making certain payments and deposit it with the government against the recipient's PAN. Common cases are salary (at slab rates), bank interest, dividends, rent, professional fees and property purchases. Under the rules as of 2025, banks deduct 10% on interest above ₹50,000 a year (₹1 lakh for senior citizens) and companies deduct 10% on dividends above ₹10,000; the rate rises to 20% if no PAN is given. The deduction appears in Form 26AS and is credited against the recipient's final tax, with any excess refunded after filing a return. The Income-tax Act 2025 gathers TDS provisions into a single section, Section 393. TDS gives the government early revenue and an audit trail. The confusion to avoid: TDS is not an extra tax; it is an advance payment of your own tax.
example: Say a resident earns ₹80,000 of fixed deposit interest in FY 2025-26. The bank deducts 10% TDS, ₹8,000, and credits ₹72,000. If the person is in the 30% slab, tax on that interest is ₹24,000 before cess, so they pay ₹16,000 more; if they have no taxable income, they claim the ₹8,000 back as a refund.
formula: TDS = Payment amount x Applicable TDS rate

short: Tax that a seller collects from the buyer on top of the price for certain transactions and deposits with the government on the buyer's behalf.
kid: When you buy a big toy from far away, the shopkeeper asks for one extra coin and puts it in the town's jar with your name on it. Later it counts towards your share.
detail: Tax collected at source (TCS) is the mirror image of TDS: the seller, or the bank sending money abroad, collects tax from the buyer at the time of the transaction and deposits it against the buyer's PAN. Under the rules as of 2025, it applies to foreign remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme above ₹10 lakh a year (generally at 20%, less for education and medical purposes), overseas tour packages, cars costing over ₹10 lakh, and sales of scrap, minerals and some forest produce. TCS is not a final cost: it shows in Form 26AS and is adjusted against your tax for the year or refunded after you file a return, and salaried people can ask their employer to count it against salary TDS. Its main purpose is to track high-value spending. In news, note that the abbreviation TCS usually means Tata Consultancy Services, not this tax.
example: Say a resident sends ₹15 lakh abroad under the LRS in FY 2025-26 to invest in foreign shares. TCS at 20% applies to the ₹5 lakh above the ₹10 lakh threshold, so the bank collects ₹1 lakh. That ₹1 lakh is credited against the person's income tax for the year, or refunded if it exceeds the tax due.
formula: TCS = Amount above the threshold x Applicable TCS rate

short: Income tax paid in instalments during the year in which the income is earned, instead of in one lump sum after the year ends.
kid: Instead of sharing all your sweets at the end of the party, you share a few at a time as you get them. That way nobody has to wait.
detail: Advance tax applies the pay-as-you-earn idea to income not fully covered by TDS, such as business profits, capital gains, rent or interest. Under the rules as of 2025, anyone whose tax for the year, after TDS and TCS, is ₹10,000 or more must pay it in four instalments: at least 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March. Shortfalls attract interest of 1% a month under Sections 234B and 234C. Resident senior citizens with no business income are exempt, and businesses using presumptive taxation may pay it all by 15 March. Corporate advance tax payments after each deadline are watched as an early read on company profits. Tax on a capital gain booked mid-year is due only from the next instalment. The confusion to avoid: advance tax is not an additional tax, just an earlier payment of the same tax.
example: Say a person expects tax of ₹2 lakh on rental and interest income for FY 2025-26, with no TDS. They should have paid ₹30,000 by 15 June, a total of ₹90,000 by 15 September, ₹1.5 lakh by 15 December and the full ₹2 lakh by 15 March. Paying it all at the end would attract interest on each shortfall.
formula: Cumulative advance tax due = Estimated tax for the year x 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% by the four due dates

short: The yearly form a taxpayer files reporting income, deductions and tax already paid, to settle the final tax bill or claim a refund.
kid: At the end of the year you write down how many sweets you got and how many you already shared. Then the grown-ups check whether you owe more or get some back.
detail: An income tax return (ITR) is the annual statement filed online with the Income Tax Department, declaring income under each head, deductions claimed, and taxes already paid through TDS, TCS, advance tax and self-assessment tax. India has several forms: ITR-1 (Sahaj) for simple salaried cases, ITR-2 for most people with capital gains, ITR-3 for business income, ITR-4 (Sugam) for presumptive income, and others for firms, companies and trusts. Under the rules as of 2025, most individuals not needing an audit must file by 31 July after the financial year, with belated or revised returns allowed until 31 December and an updated return later on paying extra tax. Filing is needed to claim refunds and carry forward losses, and lenders and visa offices often ask for it. Filing numbers are also a gauge of the formal tax base. The confusion: having TDS deducted is not the same as filing a return.
example: Say a salaried person's tax for FY 2025-26 works out to ₹81,900, but their employer deducted ₹90,000 as TDS. Filing the ITR by the due date in 2026 lets them claim the extra ₹8,100 as a refund. Without a return, the refund is never paid.
formula: Tax payable (or refund if negative) = Total tax liability - (TDS + TCS + Advance tax + Self-assessment tax)
related: Set-off and carry forward of losses

short: A certificate an Indian employer gives each employee after the year, showing salary paid and the income tax deducted from it.
kid: At the end of the year, the boss gives a note that says: here is what we paid you, and here is what we kept aside for the town.
detail: Form 16 is the TDS certificate an employer must issue for salary, by 15 June after the financial year ends under the rules as of 2025. Part A, generated from the TRACES portal, lists the employer's TAN, the employee's PAN and the tax deducted and deposited each quarter. Part B shows the salary breakup, exemptions such as HRA, the standard deduction, other deductions and the tax computed under the chosen regime. Form 16A is the quarterly certificate for TDS on other payments, such as interest, professional fees or rent. Employees use Form 16 to file their ITR, but should match it with Form 26AS and the AIS, since only tax actually deposited counts as credit. Under the 2025 Act's rules, many forms carry new numbers, but the role stays the same. The confusion to avoid: Form 16 is not a tax return; you still have to file one.
example: Say Form 16 shows gross salary of ₹14 lakh, the ₹75,000 standard deduction and taxable income of ₹13.25 lakh under the new regime for FY 2025-26. Tax is ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + ₹18,750 = ₹78,750, plus 4% cess of ₹3,150, so ₹81,900, which the employer deducted at ₹6,825 a month.

short: An annual statement on India's income tax website listing all tax deducted, collected or paid in your name during the year.
kid: The town keeps a notebook page with your name on it. Every time someone puts a coin in the jar for you, they write it down so nobody forgets.
detail: Form 26AS is the annual tax credit statement linked to a taxpayer's PAN on the income tax e-filing portal. It shows TDS and TCS reported by deductors, advance and self-assessment tax paid, and refunds. Since late 2021 the department has also published the Annual Information Statement (AIS), a much wider record built from reports by banks, registrars, brokers and others: interest, dividends, share and mutual fund trades, property purchases, foreign remittances and more. The Taxpayer Information Summary (TIS) condenses the AIS into totals by category and feeds prefilled returns. Taxpayers should reconcile their return with all three before filing, because a mismatch often triggers an automated notice; wrong entries can be challenged through AIS feedback. The confusion to avoid: you can claim credit only for TDS that appears in 26AS, since tax an employer or bank deducted but never deposited is not credited to you.
example: Say your bank paid you ₹80,000 of fixed deposit interest and deducted ₹8,000 TDS in FY 2025-26. Form 26AS shows the ₹8,000 credit and the AIS shows the ₹80,000 interest. If your return reports only salary and leaves out the interest, the mismatch is likely to bring a notice asking you to explain or pay the extra tax.

short: The year following the one in which income is earned, when that income is reported and taxed under India's 1961 tax law.
kid: You collect sweets all through this year. Next year, the grown-ups count them up and decide how many you should share.
detail: Under the Income-tax Act 1961, income earned in a financial year, called the 'previous year' and running April to March, is assessed and taxed in the following 'assessment year'. So income earned from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 belongs to FY 2025-26 and AY 2026-27, and ITR forms are labelled by AY. Students often mix the two and pick the wrong year on the portal or on a tax payment challan, which can misallocate the payment. The Income-tax Act 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, drops both terms in favour of a single 'tax year', the April-March year in which the income is earned; tax year 2026-27 is the first under the new law. Returns for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27) are still filed under the 1961 Act. Most countries simply use a tax year, though dates differ: the US uses January to December.
example: Salary earned between 1 April 2025 and 31 March 2026 is income of FY 2025-26, assessed in AY 2026-27, and its return is filed during 2026. Salary earned between 1 April 2026 and 31 March 2027 falls in tax year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act 2025, with the return filed in 2027.
formula: Assessment year = Financial year in which income is earned + 1 year (FY 2025-26 income is assessed in AY 2026-27)

short: The law that replaced India's Income-tax Act 1961 from 1 April 2026, rewriting direct tax rules in simpler language with far fewer sections.
kid: The rule book for sharing sweets got too thick and messy. So the grown-ups wrote a new, shorter book that says the same things more simply.
detail: The Income-tax Act 2025 replaced the Income-tax Act 1961, which had been amended thousands of times over six decades. A first Income Tax Bill was introduced in February 2025 and reviewed by a parliamentary select committee, then withdrawn and replaced by a revised bill that Parliament passed in August 2025; it took effect on 1 April 2026. Its aim is simplification, not new tax policy: rates, slabs and most rules carried over, but the law shrank from about 819 sections in 47 chapters to 536 sections in 23 chapters, with tables and formulas replacing long provisos. The most visible changes are a single 'tax year' in place of 'previous year' and 'assessment year', and new section numbers. Textbooks and news will keep citing 1961 section numbers for years. The confusion to avoid: income earned up to March 2026 is still governed by the 1961 Act.
example: Under the 1961 Act, income earned in FY 2025-26 is assessed in AY 2026-27; under the 2025 Act, income earned from April 2026 to March 2027 is simply tax year 2026-27. A taxpayer claiming the familiar 80C deduction now cites Section 123, and the new tax regime of Section 115BAC sits in Section 202.

short: The body under India's Finance Ministry that runs the Income Tax Department and makes rules for direct taxes such as income tax.
kid: It is like the head teacher who makes sure everyone shares their sweets fairly and on time, and explains the sharing rules when people are confused.
detail: The Central Board of Direct Taxes is a statutory body set up under the Central Boards of Revenue Act 1963, within the Department of Revenue of the Ministry of Finance. It has a chairperson and up to six members and oversees the Income Tax Department, which collects income tax, corporate tax and securities transaction tax. The CBDT frames income tax rules, notifies forms and the cost inflation index, issues circulars clarifying how the law applies, extends filing deadlines and releases direct tax collection data. Its counterpart for GST, customs and excise is the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC). Markets track its circulars because they can settle disputes, for example on how foreign investors or buybacks are taxed. The confusion to avoid: the CBDT administers the law but does not set tax rates; Parliament does that through the Finance Act.
example: In May 2025 the CBDT extended the due date for filing non-audit income tax returns for AY 2025-26 from 31 July to 15 September 2025, citing changes to the ITR forms. One notification like this moves the deadline for millions of taxpayers without any new law.

short: Tax on the profit made when you sell an asset, such as shares, mutual fund units, property or gold, for more than you paid.
kid: You buy a toy car for five coins and later sell it for eight. You give a little of the three extra coins to the town.
detail: A capital gain is the profit on selling a capital asset: the sale price minus the cost of buying it and any improvement and transfer costs. In India, gains are short-term or long-term depending on the holding period, and each is taxed differently. Under the rules from 23 July 2024, as of 2025, listed shares and equity mutual funds held over 12 months are long-term and taxed at 12.5% above a ₹1.25 lakh yearly exemption, while short-term gains on them are taxed at 20%. Most other assets need 24 months to be long-term, are taxed at 12.5% without indexation when long-term, and at slab rates when short-term; debt funds bought after March 2023 are taxed at slab rates however long they are held. This drives habits such as waiting 12 months to sell. The confusion to avoid: tax arises only on sale, not on paper gains while you hold.
example: Say an investor buys shares of ABC Ltd for ₹2 lakh and sells them two years later for ₹5 lakh in FY 2025-26. The ₹3 lakh gain is long-term; after the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, ₹1.75 lakh is taxed at 12.5%, which is ₹21,875 before cess.
formula: Capital gain = Sale price - (Cost of acquisition + Cost of improvement + Transfer expenses)
related: Set-off and carry forward of losses

short: Profit from selling an asset held only a short time, such as listed shares sold within 12 months, usually taxed at a higher rate.
kid: If you swap a toy soon after getting it and end up with more coins, you share a bigger part of the extra.
detail: Short-term capital gains (STCG) arise when an asset is sold before it qualifies as long-term. Under the rules as of 2025, the cut-off is 12 months for listed shares, equity mutual funds and other listed securities, and 24 months for most other assets such as property, gold and unlisted shares. STCG on listed equity and equity funds where securities transaction tax is paid is taxed at a flat 20% under Section 111A, raised from 15% in July 2024. STCG on other assets is added to income and taxed at slab rates. Under the new regime, the Section 87A rebate cannot be used against this tax. STCG rates matter for frequent traders and for funds that turn over their portfolios quickly. The confusion to avoid: profits from intraday trading and futures and options are usually treated as business income, not STCG.
example: Say an investor buys listed shares for ₹1 lakh and sells them six months later for ₹1.5 lakh in FY 2025-26. The ₹50,000 short-term gain is taxed at 20%, so the tax is ₹10,000 before cess, whatever the investor's slab.
formula: STCG = Sale price - Cost of acquisition - Transfer expenses (for an asset sold within the short-term holding period)

short: Profit from selling an asset held longer than a set period, such as listed shares held over 12 months, usually taxed at a lower rate.
kid: If you keep a toy for a long time before swapping it for more coins, you only need to share a small part of the extra.
detail: Long-term capital gains (LTCG) arise on assets held beyond the holding period: more than 12 months for listed shares and equity funds, and more than 24 months for most other assets, under the rules as of 2025. Since 23 July 2024, LTCG on listed equity and equity funds is taxed at 12.5% under Section 112A, with the first ₹1.25 lakh of such gains each year exempt. Other long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation, although resident individuals selling land or buildings bought before 23 July 2024 may choose 20% with indexation instead. Equity gains that built up before 31 January 2018 are grandfathered, because LTCG on listed shares was fully exempt until then. Lower LTCG rates reward patient investing, and changes to them move markets on Budget day. The confusion to avoid: the ₹1.25 lakh exemption is per person per year, not per investment.
example: Say an investor redeems equity mutual fund units held for three years, with a gain of ₹2 lakh in FY 2025-26. The first ₹1.25 lakh is exempt and the remaining ₹75,000 is taxed at 12.5%, so the tax is ₹9,375 before cess.
formula: Taxable LTCG on listed equity = Total such LTCG for the year - Annual exemption (₹1.25 lakh as of 2025)

short: Raising the purchase cost of an asset in line with inflation before working out the taxable gain, so tax falls only on the real gain.
kid: A sweet cost one coin when you were little, but now it costs two. So if you sell your old sweet for two coins, you haven't really earned anything extra.
detail: Indexation adjusts the cost of an asset for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index (CII), which the CBDT notifies each year with 2001-02 as the base of 100. The indexed cost is the original cost multiplied by the CII of the year of sale and divided by the CII of the year of purchase, so only the gain above inflation is taxed. For years, long-term gains on property, gold and debt funds were taxed at 20% with indexation. The July 2024 Budget removed indexation for transfers from 23 July 2024 and cut the rate to 12.5%, but under the rules as of 2025 resident individuals and HUFs selling land or buildings bought before that date can still pay the lower of the two calculations. Listed equity gains under Section 112A get no indexation. The confusion to avoid: indexation does not reduce the sale price; it raises the cost.
example: Say a flat bought for ₹40 lakh in a year when the CII was 200 is sold for ₹1 crore in a year when the CII is 360. Indexed cost = ₹40 lakh x 360 / 200 = ₹72 lakh, so the gain is ₹28 lakh and tax at 20% is ₹5.6 lakh. Without indexation, tax at 12.5% on the ₹60 lakh gain is ₹7.5 lakh, so an eligible seller would choose indexation.
formula: Indexed cost = Original cost x (CII of the year of sale / CII of the year of purchase)

term: Set-off and carry forward of losses
short: Tax rules that let you subtract a loss from other income or gains, and carry unused losses into future years to reduce later tax.
kid: If you lose two sweets today and win five tomorrow, your real win is only three. If you can't use a loss yet, you save it for later.
detail: Set-off means using a loss to reduce income in the same year; carry forward means taking an unused loss into later years. Indian rules, as of 2025, are strict. A short-term capital loss can be set off against both short- and long-term gains, but a long-term capital loss only against long-term gains, and capital losses never against salary or other heads. Business losses can reduce most income except salary, while speculative losses, such as from intraday trading, only reduce speculative profits. Unused capital and ordinary business losses can be carried forward for eight years and speculative losses for four, only if the return is filed on time. In the old regime, a house property loss can reduce other income by up to ₹2 lakh a year. These rules underpin tax-loss harvesting and companies' deferred tax assets. The confusion to avoid: a capital loss cannot cut tax on your salary.
example: Say an investor books a ₹2 lakh long-term capital loss on shares this year and has no long-term gains, so they report it in a return filed on time and carry it forward. Next year they make ₹3 lakh of long-term gains on listed equity; after setting off the loss only ₹1 lakh remains, which is within the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption under the rules as of 2025, so no tax is due.

short: Selling investments that are showing a loss so the loss is booked, reducing the tax due on gains made elsewhere in the same year.
kid: You won five marbles in one game and lost two in another. If you count both games, you only won three, so you share less.
detail: Tax-loss harvesting means deliberately selling investments trading below their purchase price to realise a capital loss, which is then set off against capital gains, in India usually before the financial year ends on 31 March. Investors often buy the same or a similar investment back so their portfolio barely changes. Short-term losses can offset both short- and long-term gains, long-term losses only long-term gains, and unused losses can be carried forward for eight years. A related Indian practice, also called tax harvesting, is booking long-term equity gains up to the ₹1.25 lakh yearly exemption and buying back, which raises the cost base tax-free. The US blocks quick buybacks through a 30-day wash-sale rule; India has no explicit equivalent as of 2025, but trades should be genuine. The confusion to avoid: harvesting reduces or defers tax; it does not make a losing investment profitable.
example: Say an investor has ₹2 lakh of short-term gains on listed shares in FY 2025-26 and holds another stock, bought five months ago, showing an unrealised short-term loss of ₹80,000. Selling it before 31 March cuts net short-term gains to ₹1.2 lakh, so tax at 20% falls from ₹40,000 to ₹24,000, a saving of ₹16,000 before cess.
formula: Tax saved = Harvested loss x Tax rate on the gains it offsets
related: Set-off and carry forward of losses

short: A small tax charged on every purchase or sale of shares, derivatives and equity fund units on Indian stock exchanges.
kid: Each time you swap a trading card at the school card table, you drop a tiny crumb of cookie into the teacher's jar.
detail: Securities transaction tax (STT) is a tax on the value of trades in listed securities on recognised Indian stock exchanges, introduced in October 2004. The exchange collects it through brokers and passes it to the government; the CBDT administers it as a direct tax. Under the rates as of 2025 (in force from October 2024), equity delivery trades pay 0.1% on both buy and sell, intraday trades 0.025% on the sell side, futures 0.02% on the sale value and options 0.1% of the premium on sale. Paying STT is a condition for the concessional capital gains rates on listed equity. Governments have raised STT on derivatives to cool speculative trading, so changes hit broker and exchange stocks. Investors cannot deduct STT when computing capital gains, though active traders can treat it as a business expense. The confusion to avoid: STT is charged whether you make a profit or a loss.
example: Say an investor buys shares worth ₹1 lakh for delivery and later sells them for ₹1.2 lakh. At 0.1%, STT is ₹100 on the purchase and ₹120 on the sale, ₹220 in all, under the rates as of 2025. A trader selling futures worth ₹10 lakh pays 0.02%, or ₹200.
formula: STT = Transaction value x STT rate for that type of trade

short: How dividends are taxed; in India since April 2020, shareholders pay tax on dividends at their own income tax rates, replacing a company-paid tax.
kid: When the lemonade stand shares its extra coins with its owners, each owner then puts a few of those coins in the town jar.
detail: Dividend taxation covers how profits paid out to shareholders are taxed. Until March 2020, Indian companies paid a dividend distribution tax (DDT) of 15% on a grossed-up basis plus surcharge and cess, an effective rate of about 20.56%, and most shareholders then received dividends tax-free. The Finance Act 2020 abolished DDT, so dividends are now added to the shareholder's income and taxed at slab rates, with surcharge capped at 15%. Under the rules as of 2025, companies deduct 10% TDS for resident shareholders when dividends from that company exceed ₹10,000 in a year, while non-residents face 20% or a lower treaty rate. The shift made dividends less attractive for high-income investors and, for a time, made buybacks more popular. Many countries tax 'qualified' dividends at lower rates. The confusion to avoid: TDS is not the final tax; someone in the 30% slab owes the balance.
example: Say an investor in the 30% slab receives ₹50,000 of dividends from ABC Ltd in FY 2025-26. ABC deducts 10% TDS, ₹5,000. Tax on the dividend is ₹15,000 plus 4% cess, so ₹15,600, and the investor pays the remaining ₹10,600 when filing the return.
formula: Tax still payable on dividends = Dividend income x Marginal tax rate (plus surcharge and cess) - TDS already deducted

short: The tax charged when a company buys back its own shares, either on the company or on the shareholders who sell, depending on the rules.
kid: The lemonade stand buys back an owner's card and pays some coins. Then someone has to put a few of those coins in the town jar.
detail: Buyback tax is how India taxes a company's repurchase of its own shares, and the rules have changed often. From 2013 for unlisted companies and from July 2019 for listed ones, the company paid tax of 20% plus surcharge and cess, about 23.3%, on the amount by which the buyback price exceeded the original issue price, and shareholders were exempt. Being cheaper than dividends for large holders, buybacks grew popular after DDT ended. Under the rules as of 2025, applying from 1 October 2024, the whole buyback payment is treated as a dividend taxed in the shareholder's hands at slab rates, and the original cost of the shares becomes a capital loss that can be set off against other capital gains. These rules change often, so check the latest Finance Act. The confusion to avoid: under the 2024 rules the whole payment, not just the profit, counts as dividend.
example: Say that under the rules from October 2024 an investor tenders 100 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹500 each, which they bought at ₹300. The full ₹50,000 is taxed as dividend at their slab rate, while the ₹30,000 cost becomes a capital loss they can set off against capital gains or carry forward. In the 30% slab, tax on the dividend is ₹15,000 before cess.
related: Set-off and carry forward of losses

short: Credit a business gets for the GST it paid on its purchases, which it subtracts from the GST it collects on its own sales.
kid: You paid one sticker to the town when you bought lemons, and your customers gave you three stickers. You only hand over two more, because one was already paid.
detail: Input tax credit (ITC) is the mechanism that lets GST tax only the value added at each stage. A registered business deducts the GST paid on inputs, input services and capital goods used in its business from the GST due on its sales, and pays only the difference. To claim it, the business must hold a valid tax invoice and have received the goods or services, and the supplier must have reported the invoice so it shows in the buyer's GSTR-2B and paid the tax. Some credits are blocked, such as on most cars, food and personal consumption. ITC removes the cascading tax on tax of older indirect taxes, and claims on fake invoices are a major area of GST fraud. The confusion to avoid: ITC is set off against output tax, not paid out as a refund. In news, ITC usually means the company ITC Ltd.
example: Say a manufacturer buys inputs worth ₹1 lakh plus 18% GST of ₹18,000, and sells its goods for ₹1.5 lakh plus 18% GST of ₹27,000. It claims ₹18,000 as input tax credit and pays only ₹9,000 to the government, which is 18% of the ₹50,000 of value it added.
formula: Net GST payable = Output GST on sales - Eligible input tax credit

short: A tax charged on goods brought into a country, and sometimes on goods sent out, usually as a percentage of their value.
kid: When a toy comes from another town, the gatekeeper asks for a few coins before letting it in. That makes the toys made at home look a bit cheaper.
detail: Customs duty is a tax on imports, and occasionally exports. In India it is levied under the Customs Act 1962 at rates set in the Customs Tariff Act 1975 and administered by the CBIC. On imports the main parts are basic customs duty (BCD), surcharges and cesses such as the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess, and IGST charged on the value including duty. BCD is calculated on the assessable value, broadly the cost, insurance and freight (CIF) value of the goods. Customs duty raises revenue and shields domestic industry, so Budget changes move sectors such as electronics, gold, solar and autos. Extra duties like anti-dumping and safeguard duties target unfair or surging imports. The confusion to avoid: a GST-registered importer can claim the IGST paid as input tax credit, but basic customs duty is a final cost. In news, tariff is often used as a synonym.
example: Say an importer brings in goods with a CIF value of ₹10 lakh, attracting 10% BCD (₹1 lakh), a 10% social welfare surcharge on that BCD (₹10,000) and 18% IGST on ₹11.1 lakh (₹1,99,800). The total paid at the port is ₹3,09,800, of which the ₹1,99,800 of IGST can be claimed back as input tax credit.
formula: Basic customs duty = Assessable value (broadly CIF value) x BCD rate
